Abstract
                Context
                As a novel coronavirus swept the world in early 2020, thousands of software developers began working from home. Many did so on short notice, under difficult and stressful conditions.
              
                Objective
                This study investigates the effects of the pandemic on developers’ wellbeing and productivity.
              
                Method
                A questionnaire survey was created mainly from existing, validated scales and translated into 12 languages. The data was analyzed using non-parametric inferential statistics and structural equation modeling.
              
                Results
                The questionnaire received 2225 usable responses from 53 countries. Factor analysis supported the validity of the scales and the structural model achieved a good fit (CFI = 0.961, RMSEA = 0.051, SRMR = 0.067). Confirmatory results include: (1) the pandemic has had a negative effect on developers’ wellbeing and productivity; (2) productivity and wellbeing are closely related; (3) disaster preparedness, fear related to the pandemic and home office ergonomics all affect wellbeing or productivity. Exploratory analysis suggests that: (1) women, parents and people with disabilities may be disproportionately affected; (2) different people need different kinds of support.
              
                Conclusions
                To improve employee productivity, software companies should focus on maximizing employee wellbeing and improving the ergonomics of employees’ home offices. Women, parents and disabled persons may require extra support.

Abstract

Context
When the novel coronavirus spread globally in early 2020, thousands of software developers started working from home, often on very short notice and in difficult, stressful circumstances.

Objective
This study examines how the pandemic affected developers’ wellbeing and productivity.

Method
The questionnaire survey was built mainly from existing validated scales and translated into 12 languages. Data were analyzed with non-parametric inferential statistics and structural equation modeling.

Results
The questionnaire yielded 2225 usable responses from 53 countries. Factor analysis confirmed the scales’ validity, and the structural model showed a good fit (CFI = 0.961, RMSEA = 0.051, SRMR = 0.067). Confirmatory findings show that: (1) the pandemic negatively affected developers’ wellbeing and productivity; (2) productivity and wellbeing are closely linked; (3) disaster preparedness, pandemic-related fear, and home-office ergonomics all influence wellbeing or productivity. Exploratory analysis indicates that: (1) women, parents, and people with disabilities may be disproportionately affected; (2) different individuals need different types of support.

Conclusions
To improve employee productivity, software companies should prioritize employee wellbeing and better home-office ergonomics. Women, parents, and disabled persons may need additional support.
